title: DoR and DoD at project and team level
blurb: Place the Definitions of Ready and Done inside the quality practice, and say what is set at project level and what at team level.
question: During initiation, the board asks for criteria that every user story must meet before any team starts it, and criteria that all work must meet before users receive it. Which artifacts are these, and where are they agreed?

teach.h: Two quality artifacts with two levels
teach.body: The Definition of Ready (DoR) and Definition of Done (DoD) are artifacts of the quality practice. The DoR sets the criteria an item must meet before work begins; the DoD sets the criteria it must meet to be considered complete. PRINCE2 Agile uses them at two levels: product-wide definitions for the whole project, and a team DoD that each delivery team applies to its own work.

teach.h: Done or not done, at every level
teach.body: Whatever the level, the rule is the same: something is either done or not done; there is no 'almost done'. A DoD may include review, validation or approval by stakeholders, and work that still has defects is not done. If a story is partly finished before a review, it is split: the done part moves to done and the rest returns to the backlog to be reprioritized.

teach.h: How the definitions are used through the project

steps.label: Team planning
steps.sub: story refinement: what counts as done

teach.body: Brackenford Community Health is redesigning its patient appointment letters. In the project initiation workshop, project manager Daniel Osei leads the project DoR topic: no story starts without plain-language wording approved and a measurable reading-age criterion. The project DoD requires a clinical review and a check by patient representatives. Product owner Aisha Khan's team adds its own DoD in the product backlog: printed proof checked and template saved.

teach.text: Project DoR and project DoD have their OWN topics in the project initiation workshop. They are not set under the 'management approaches' topic. And the team DoD sits with the product backlog (PO), not the project backlog (CPO).

teach.h: The DoD in contracts and roles
teach.body: An agreed DoD can also support agile contracts through the commercial management approach. In delivery, the tester reviews products against acceptance or quality criteria and the team DoD. In the team planning workshop, the user story refinement topic makes acceptance criteria clear and testable and aligns on what qualifies as done for each story.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table 7.3, Table 13.13

items: DoR and DoD are quality practice artifacts (Table 9.1).
Project DoR and project DoD: own topics in the project initiation workshop (Table 13.7).
Project definitions come from the quality management approach and appear in the project backlog.
Project DoD: quality needed before work is handed to users and the CPO.
Team DoD: included or linked in the product backlog; the tester checks against it.
Done or not done; defects mean not done; split partly done stories.

summary: You can now place the DoR and DoD inside the quality practice and say which definitions are agreed at project level in the project initiation workshop. You can also say that the team DoD sits with the product backlog and is checked by the tester.

A.q: To which practice do the Definition of Ready and Definition of Done belong as artifacts?
A.why: The DoR and DoD are listed among the quality practice artifacts (9.3.2, Table 9.1).

whyNot.0: Plans artifacts include the release map, team plan and work package as a set of user stories.
whyNot.1: Progress artifacts include the team and project dashboards and the exception report.
whyNot.3: Issues artifacts include the issue register and issue report.

A.q: Where is the team Definition of Done included or linked?
A.why: A product backlog in PRINCE2 Agile includes or links to the team Definition of Done (8.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: The project backlog shows or links the project DoR and DoD, not the team DoD.
whyNot.2: The release map is the project and stage plan.
whyNot.3: The project canvas is the one-page business justification.

A.q: A design has been built but still has two known defects at the review. How should it be classed?
A.why: Something is either done or not done, and work with defects is not done (9.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Ready describes an item meeting the DoR before work starts, not finished work.
whyNot.1: PRINCE2 Agile states there is no 'almost done' in agile.
whyNot.2: Work with defects fails the DoD, so it cannot be accepted as complete.

B.q: In the project initiation workshop, under which topic are product-wide criteria for starting work on user stories agreed?
B.why: The project DoR topic lists product-overarching criteria needed to start development work on work packages or user stories (Table 13.7).

whyNot.1: The management approaches topic co-creates the approaches; readiness criteria have their own topic.
whyNot.2: The project DoD topic covers criteria for work to be done and acceptable, not ready to start.
whyNot.3: Persona definition describes typical users of the product.

B.q: The project Definition of Done creates a shared understanding of the quality needed before work is handed to whom?
B.why: The project DoD sets criteria for work to be done and acceptable to user needs, before it is handed over to users or the CPO (Table 13.7).

whyNot.0: Handing work to development relates to the project DoR, not the DoD.
whyNot.2: The board directs the project; the DoD concerns acceptance by users and the CPO.
whyNot.3: The PM and project support manage and administer; they are not the acceptors.

B.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. The project DoR and DoD are shown or linked in the project backlog.
2. The team DoD is agreed by the board in directing a project.
3. The tester reviews products against the team DoD.
4. A partly done story is recorded as done if most criteria are met.
B.why: The project backlog shows or links the project DoR and DoD (1), and the tester reviews products against acceptance criteria and the team DoD (3) (8.3.2.1, Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the team DoD sits with the team's product backlog, not with a board decision.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: the board does not set the team DoD, and partly done stories are split, not recorded as done.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: there is no 'almost done'; the story is split.

C.q: Which workshop agrees the project Definition of Ready, and in which process is it held?
options: Project initiation workshop; initiating a project
Team planning workshop; managing product delivery
Starting up workshop; starting up a project
Project kickoff workshop; controlling a stage
C.why: The project DoR is a topic of the project initiation workshop, which supports initiating a project (Table 13.7).

whyNot.1: Team planning refines stories and acceptance criteria for an iteration; it does not set the project DoR.
whyNot.2: The starting up workshop covers roles, lessons, initiation planning, risks and refining the plan.
whyNot.3: The kickoff workshop builds the team and dashboards and belongs to initiation, not controlling a stage.

C.q: A product owner's team wants a shared rule for when its own stories are complete. Where should it be kept, and who checks products against it?
C.why: The team DoD is included in or linked from the product backlog, and the tester reviews products against it (8.3.2.1, Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: The project backlog holds the project-level definitions, and assurance monitors governance, not each product.
whyNot.1: The quality register records quality activities and results, not the team's DoD.
whyNot.3: The team plan is the iteration task plan, and the team coach does not check products against the DoD.

C.q: In the team planning workshop, which topic aligns the team on what qualifies as done for each story, and what does it examine?
options: Effort estimation; story points per story
C.why: User story refinement examines acceptance criteria so they are clear and testable and aligns on what qualifies as done (Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Iteration planning selects stories for the next iteration and finalizes the team plan.
whyNot.1: Effort estimation builds a shared view of each story's complexity and effort.
whyNot.2: Product backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes requirements using MoSCoW.

reteach.title: House rules and room rules
reteach.question: How can there be a Definition of Done for the project and another one for each team?

blocks.body: A hotel has house rules for every room: fire safety checked, linen changed. Each housekeeping team then adds its own room checklist: towels folded their way, minibar counted. The project DoR and DoD are the house rules, agreed in the project initiation workshop. The team DoD is the room checklist, kept with each team's product backlog.

blocks.text: Starting rules are the DoR; finishing rules are the DoD. Product-wide rules are project level (initiation workshop); one team's rules are the team DoD (product backlog).

explain.body: Both definitions are artifacts of the quality practice. The DoR guards the start of work; the DoD guards its completion.

test.q: What does the Definition of Ready specify?
options: Criteria an item must meet to be complete
Criteria an item must meet before work begins
The order in which items are delivered
The users who will accept the product
test.why: The DoR is a shared agreement on the criteria an item must meet before work begins (9.3.2.1).

whyNot.2: Delivery order comes from prioritization and the release map.
whyNot.3: Who accepts the project product is named in the project backlog.

explain.body: The project DoR and project DoD are agreed as separate topics of the project initiation workshop. They come from the quality management approach and appear in the project backlog.

test.q: Which artifact shows or links the project Definition of Ready and Definition of Done?
test.why: The project backlog shows or links the project DoR and DoD and names who accepts the project product (8.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: The product backlog links the team DoD.
whyNot.1: The team dashboard reports team progress.
whyNot.2: The release map is the plan of releases and iterations.

explain.body: Each product backlog includes or links the team DoD. The tester reviews products against acceptance criteria and the team DoD.

test.q: Which role reviews products against acceptance criteria and the team Definition of Done?
test.why: Testers review products against acceptance or quality criteria and the team DoD (Table 7.2).

whyNot.1: The team coach helps one or two teams self-manage and facilitates workshops.
whyNot.2: Project support gives administrative help and updates dashboards.
whyNot.3: The agile coach works across the organization on systemic blockers.

explain.body: There is no 'almost done'. A partly done story is split: the done part moves to done and the rest goes back to the backlog for reprioritization.

test.q: A story is partly finished at the review. What happens to the unfinished part?
options: It moves to the next release
test.why: The unfinished part moves back into the backlog to await reprioritization (9.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: There is no 'almost done' in agile.
whyNot.1: Iterations are timeboxed; unfinished work is not carried as done.
whyNot.3: It goes back to the backlog for reprioritization rather than straight into a release.
